column3: Affirms that what is promised is true, directly opposing the focus's repeated dismissal of its fulfillment as remote.
The next generation in the same surah extends the recurring messenger-and-rejection pattern behind the focus's speakers.
Treats God's promise as one not broken, but its prayer context adds little to the focused denial of resurrection.
Declares that what is promised will occur, supplying a concise counterclaim to the focus's rejection.
The call to worship forms local narrative context for the disbelief expressed in the focus.
Contrasts deceptive promises with a promise that can be trusted, helping distinguish the deniers' dismissal from a valid challenge.
Identifies the promised reality with the Day of Account, specifying the future event the focus puts at a distance.
The earlier Noah narrative establishes a local pattern of prophetic address but does not itself develop the promised resurrection.
Affirms the truth of God's promise on the basis of divine ownership, directly answering the focus's repudiation.
Shows the promised Hell as encountered reality, supplying a concrete outcome of treating the warning as distant.
An earlier community's objection to a human messenger parallels local resistance, but not the specific promise in the focus.
Warns that even part of a prophet's promised outcome may reach the rejecters, a general caution against dismissal.
Places provision and what is promised beyond present sight, clarifying why unseen promise need not be judged by immediate availability.
The charge of madness is local rejection context without further account of the promised event.
Calls God's promise true, but concerns the scope of Noah's family rather than denial of resurrection.
God's effective will supplies a broad ground for fulfillment, without identifying the promise rejected in the focus.
Noah's appeal after being called a liar continues the local resistance pattern but adds no promise-specific detail.
Explicitly denies that God can fail the promise, directly contesting the focus's claim that it is impossibly remote.
The rhetorical question about chosen privileges does not clarify the promised resurrection.
The same leaders deny the meeting of the Hereafter, establishing the unbelieving stance that culminates in the focus.
Faithfulness in keeping a promise offers a general contrast to the focus's assumption that a promise can be disregarded.
Not completing a commanded task does not illuminate the promised resurrection.
The warning against obeying a human messenger is nearby denial context but does not address the promised outcome.
The demand to know when the promise will come closely parallels treating its delayed arrival as grounds for disbelief.
A fixed appointment for the destruction of unjust towns gives only a broad analogy of divinely timed outcomes.
The immediate preceding question states the promised emergence after death and decay that 23:36 rejects as far-fetched.
The son's scornful refusal of the promised rising, labeled old tales, closely mirrors the focus's dismissive response.
Consuming inheritance greedily does not clarify the rejected promise.
The immediate continuation denies resurrection outright, making explicit the proposition dismissed in 23:36.
The prior warning makes judgment an announced consequence rather than an unforeseen event, though it is less specific than the focus.
Presents promised reward as granted reality for the repentant, offering a positive counterpart to the focus's dismissal.
The immediate accusation that the messenger fabricated a lie explains why the speakers treat the promise as remote.
The prayer treats what is promised as a real event that may be shown, countering the focus's rejection of it.
States that what is promised is coming and cannot be escaped, directly answering the focus's language of remoteness.
Noah's appeal for help repeats the local reaction to denial but adds no detail about the promise.
A promise of forgiveness and reward is a distant thematic parallel, not the resurrection promise at issue.
Distinguishes nearness or delay of what is promised from knowledge of its fixed term, directly bearing on the focus's distance claim.
The announced near regret gives the local narrative a reversal of the speakers' claim that the warning is remote.
Competing promises about poverty and forgiveness illustrate future-directed trust, but not the resurrection claim.
Mutual waiting provides only a general posture of deferred outcome.
The succession of later generations continues the local historical pattern without developing the promise.
Affirms the power to show what was promised, though its immediate referent is a local threatened outcome.
The question about cultivation does not clarify the promised resurrection.
Fixed communal terms qualify the focus's claim of remoteness by locating outcomes in an appointed timing.
The resurrected recognize that their awakening is what the Merciful promised, directly reversing denial into recognition.
Admits uncertainty about whether what is promised is near or far while preserving its announced reality.
Repeated rejection of messengers supplies a broad local pattern but no specific resurrection development.
Breaking a human promise produces hypocrisy until meeting God, a secondary contrast with trust in divine promise.
The description of chosen fruit does not explain the focus.
The destruction of the denying people gives the local rejection narrative an actual consequence, though not resurrection itself.
Says the unseen promise is coming, directly opposing the focus's treatment of the promised reality as impossibly distant.
Commands deniers toward the reality they denied, supplying an enacted consequence of the focus's stance.
Affirms God's true promise and the eventual return to Him, but repeats earlier fulfillment evidence more generally.
Names the greatest terror as the promised day, specifying the eschatological arrival rejected in the focus.
Records people calling God's and the messenger's promise mere delusion, closely paralleling the focus's contemptuous dismissal.
States that the deniers see it as far away, the closest verbal and conceptual parallel to the focus's repeated remoteness claim.
Affirms the true promise of enduring reward, but adds a general positive result already represented by stronger cards.
Nearness of Paradise contrasts with the focus's distance claim only indirectly.
An experienced fulfillment of a promise supports divine reliability in a different narrative setting.
The promised day supplies a compact eschatological referent for the focus's rejected promise.
The same surah has deniers call the long-repeated promise old tales, strongly clarifying the historicalized dismissal in the focus.
Promise of Paradise to the steadfast is a positive future counterpart but not the disputed resurrection claim.
The true promise of lasting gardens broadly contrasts with rejection, but is redundant after more direct promise affirmations.
Threatening travelers on the path is a different use of promise language.
False mutual promises among idolaters offer a broad contrast with divine promise, but no direct resurrection connection.
Hell as a common appointment gives a general consequence without clarifying the focus's denial.
Fulfillment despite the messenger's limited observation is relevant to delay, but is less direct than the nearness and timing cards.
The Sabbath punishment as a warning does not clarify the focus.
The repeated challenge asking when the promise will come closely parallels disbelief based on demanded timing, though it repeats 27:71.
Hard hearts and stones do not clarify the promised resurrection.
Patience grounded in God's true promise offers general counsel but adds little after direct affirmations.
A personal promise concerning Abraham's father is unrelated to the focus's eschatological claim.
Separates the messenger's lifetime from the time of fulfillment, a secondary answer to judging the promise by delay.
Confirmation of earlier scripture does not clarify the promised resurrection.
The true promise of Paradise is a general future outcome, redundant with more direct eschatological cards.
Scriptural confirmation and good news do not address the focus.
A promised, requested Paradise describes reward but does not clarify why the focus calls the promise far away.
Confirmation of the Torah by the Gospel uses different language and context.
Seeing the promised punishment or Hour eventually reverses present delusion, but repeats stronger fulfillment cards.
Recognition and rejection of a scripture do not clarify the focus's promised resurrection.
The demand for the date of the promise closely parallels the focus's refusal to accept an unseen future, though it repeats 27:71 and 34:29.
Casting scripture behind one's back does not explain the focus.
Records doubt about the true promise and the Hour itself, directly matching the focus's denial of the promised resurrection.
The prophets' covenant concerns confirming a messenger, not the focus's promise.
A delayed good promise and a broken appointment offer only an indirect analogy to the focus's claimed remoteness.
Command to believe confirming revelation does not clarify the rejected promise.
Contrasts God's fulfilled true promise with Satan's failed promise after judgment, reinforcing the reliability the focus denies.
Confirmation of the Torah and altered law do not clarify the focus.
The unbroken promise of gardens broadly supports fulfillment but is redundant and less focused.
The threatened punishment before a command's execution does not clarify resurrection.
Secret wrongdoing and Hell do not explain the focus's distance claim.
Renouncing false worship after clear proofs does not clarify the promised resurrection.
A book confirming prior scripture does not address the focus.
The prayer for pardon and manageable burdens does not clarify the promise.
The detailed Paradise promised to the mindful is a general future reward, not the disputed resurrection event.
A threatened earthly replacement after persecutors is only a broad warning parallel.
The demand for clear authority from human messengers does not clarify the focus.
Communal reconciliation and rescue from the Fire do not address the promised resurrection.
Creation and sovereign command broadly ground divine capacity, but do not specifically develop the focus.
The two groups confirm that each found God's promise true, showing the ultimate realization the focus rejects.
The direct divine counterstatement that it is seen as near completes and reverses the focus's repeated declaration that it is far.
Calls return after death and becoming dust a far return, an especially close formulation of the focus's dismissive distance claim.
Places death immediately before the later resurrection, supplying the sequence whose promised completion the focus rejects.
Explicitly declares resurrection on the Day of Resurrection, providing the surah's direct assertion behind the promise dismissed at 23:36.
The same surah repeats the objection that dust and bones cannot be resurrected, closely matching the denial voiced around the focus.
Directly rejects the claim that people will not be resurrected and joins resurrection to being informed of deeds.
Records the emphatic claim that God will not resurrect the dead, a direct denial of the promise at issue.
States that resurrection will make disputed truth clear and expose the deniers' falsehood, directly answering their rejection.
Asks whether scattered bones and dust can become a new creation, a close restatement of the objection preceding the focus.
Identifies denial of resurrection after becoming bones and dust as a reason for punishment, directly linking the objection to consequence.
Argues that the Creator of the heavens and earth can recreate people, directly answering the claimed impossibility of the promise.
Records the incredulous question whether one will be brought forth alive after death, closely paralleling the focus's scorn.
Answers resurrection denial by recalling the first creation from nothing.
Affirms that the Hour is coming and that God will resurrect those in graves, directly specifying the promised event.
States that creating and resurrecting all people is as easy as one soul, directly answering doubt about resurrection.
Records the objection that being lost in the earth prevents a new creation, a direct counterpart to the focus's denial.
Reports ridicule of the message that completely scattered bodies will become a new creation.
Raises the exact challenge of who can give life to decayed bones, making explicit the reasoning behind the focus's dismissal.
Answers that the original Creator gives the bones life, directly rebutting the resurrection objection.
Argues that the Creator of the heavens and earth is able to create people again, reinforcing the response to the focus.
Asks whether people become resurrected after death, dust, and bones, closely matching the disputed promise.
Uses the reviving of dead earth as an explicit sign that its giver of life can give life to the dead.
Connects reviving dead land with people's future emergence, an explicit created-world analogue for the promise.
Argues that the Creator of the heavens and earth can give life to the dead, directly answering resurrection denial.
Counters doubt about a new creation by recalling the first creation.
Attributes the later creation to God, directly grounding the promised restoration.
Records the question whether people and their ancestors will be resurrected after becoming dust and bones.
Answers that the first and last generations will be gathered at an appointed known day, specifying the promise's timing and scope.
Recalls God's creation of people as the basis for challenging their refusal to affirm the promised outcome.
States divine power to replace people and produce them in an unknown form, directly bearing on re-creation after death.
Appeals to the first creation as a reason to recognize the possibility of renewed creation.
Asks whether a person thinks God will not assemble his bones, directly confronting the denial behind the focus.
Concludes that the Creator is able to give life to the dead.
Records the question whether people will really be restored, a concise direct counterpart to the focus's rejection.
Specifies the objection as restoration after becoming decayed bones.
Traces life, death, renewed life, and return to God, providing a compact sequence underlying resurrection.
The restoration after a hundred years gives a narrated sign of how God gives life after death.
States that people are brought from earth, returned to it, and brought forth again.
Uses human development and dead earth revived by rain as signs that God can resurrect the dead.
Points from originating creation to repeating it as an answer to doubt about resurrection.
States that God originates creation, then repeats it, and that people return to Him.
Describes repeating creation as easy for God, supplying a direct capacity argument.
Links revival of dead earth to God's giving life to the dead.
Explicitly compares reviving dead land to the resurrection.
The trumpet scene and universal rising provide the realized eschatological setting of the promise.
Names the Day of Decision as an appointed time, qualifying any assumption that delay negates the promise.
Depicts the trumpet and people arriving in groups, a concrete collective fulfillment scene.
The graves being overturned supplies a concise image of the emergence denied in the focus.
